text: Cleaning fixes the problems you found. Validation proves the data now meets your expectations, and keeps proving it every time new data arrives. In T-SQL you relied on constraints — primary key, not null, check, foreign key. A pandas DataFrame enforces none of those, so you write the checks yourself. Done well, they turn silent data problems into loud, specific failures.

Here's five illustrative order rows with several deliberate problems baked in, plus a customers table. Order 5003 appears twice. One amount is negative. Customer 999 doesn't actually exist in the customers table. And one order date is set all the way out in 2099.

Five families of checks, each one line of pandas. Unique — is underscore unique on order underscore id, the equivalent of a primary key, comes back False, because of that duplicate. Complete — notna dot all for amount, the equivalent of not null. In range — between 0 and 10000 dot all, the equivalent of a check constraint, comes back False because of the negative amount; a missing value isn't between anything either, so NaN fails this too. Allowed values — isin against a fixed list of statuses. And related — isin against the customers table's key, the equivalent of a foreign key, which fails because customer 999 doesn't exist.

A bare False tells you something's wrong but not what. Negate the check and use it as a filter instead. Negate the amount-between check, and you get back exactly the row with the negative amount, order 5002. Filter for duplicated order ids with keep equals False, and you get back both rows of order 5003, side by side. This is the output you actually hand to whoever owns the source system.

Put every rule into one function that returns a named True-False result. Build a dictionary where each key is a plain-English rule name and each value is the one-line check itself — order id is unique, no missing amount, amount between 0 and 10000, customer id exists — then wrap it in a pandas Series. Running it on this sample data returns a readable report, one row per rule, each one clearly True or False.

Call validate, then filter the report for everything that failed, and turn those failing rule names into a list. Assert that the list is empty, with a message that includes exactly which rules broke. Here, that assertion actually fires — Validation failed, naming order id is unique, amount between 0 and 10000, customer id exists, and no future dates, all at once. Assert stops the notebook or the script right there, so bad data never flows forward into a model or a dashboard.

A few habits make this actually work in practice. Fail fast — validate immediately after loading, and again after every major transformation, not just once at the end. Show the rows, not only a count of failures, so whoever's debugging can see exactly what broke. And keep every rule in one place, like that validate function, so the rules evolve naturally as the data does. Libraries like pandera and Great Expectations build on this exact same idea with richer reporting, if you ever want to go further.

To recap: validation replaces the constraints a database would normally give you for free. Five families cover most of it — unique, complete, in range, allowed values, and related. Is underscore unique, notna, between, and isin cover most checks directly; negate them to get the bad rows. A validate function plus assert makes failures loud and specific.
